query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, dense diffusion‐barrier coating (such as a silicide or advanced ceramic layer) to boride‐based components will significantly improve their resistance to molten‐aluminum corrosion by inhibiting interdiffusion and chemical attack at the interface during hot-dip aluminum plating.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride‐based components currently used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment without any additional surface modification.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, dense diffusion‐barrier coating (e.g., a silicide or advanced ceramic layer) via a controlled deposition technique (such as physical vapor deposition or pack cementation).
generation.conditions: Components exposed directly to molten aluminum at temperatures above 660°C under prolonged contact during the plating process.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an intact, adherent protective interface layer between the boride substrate and the molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The coating serves as a diffusion barrier, reducing the interdiffusion of aluminum into the boride substrate and limiting the chemical reactions that cause corrosion. This physical isolation minimizes the exposure of the vulnerable boride phase to the aggressive molten aluminum environment.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coated components will exhibit a significantly lower rate of corrosion (e.g., reduced weight loss and improved microstructural integrity) compared to the uncoated baseline, thereby extending their service life in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components without any diffusion-barrier coating.
generation.boundary: The protective effects are expected to remain effective only as long as the coating remains intact, adherent, and chemically stable at or above the operational temperatures encountered during the plating process.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvement and the long-term durability of the coating under cyclic thermal and chemical stresses remain uncertain until validated by empirical testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical boride-based component samples. Apply the proposed thin diffusion-barrier coating to one set while leaving the other set uncoated as the baseline. Expose both sets to molten aluminum at a controlled temperature (e.g., 680°C) for a pre-determined duration under identical conditions. Post-exposure, perform quantitative assessments of corrosion through weight loss measurements, cross-sectional microstructural analysis (using SEM/EDS), and phase composition determination.
measurements: Weight loss or gain per unit area
SEM/EDS analysis of the coating and substrate interface
Phase identification via XRD or similar technique
Adhesion integrity tests of the coating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or higher weight loss and evidence of coating degradation) compared to the uncoated samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. The comprehensive effect of the mixing of various main elements endows the high entropy alloy with high entropy effect in thermodynamics, lattice distortion effect in structure, hysteresis diffusion effect in dynamics, and “cocktail” effect in performance [ [1] , [2] ]. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. decision.trend: Over the past several years, intense research has explored how to improve extreme-environment performance by primarily adjusting bulk compositions and processing methods in refractory and high‐entropy alloy systems. In these studies, researchers first attempted to optimize mechanical strength and oxidation resistance through modifications of alloy chemistry, thermomechanical treatments, and microstructural refinement. Later works shifted focus to surface and interfacial modifications – for example, the use of silicide coatings via pack cementation has proven effective in enhancing oxidation resistance by forming a protective barrier. However, when it comes to molten-corrosion environments, particularly for components exposed to aggressive, high-temperature molten aluminum, the traditional bulk design strategies have not yet delivered sufficiently robust corrosion control.
decision.unsolved: Despite advances in bulk alloy design and processing methods, the direct exposure of boride-based components to molten aluminum in hot-dip plating remains a critical vulnerability. The open question is how to best shield the boride material from the chemically aggressive and thermally challenging aluminum melt using a single, targeted intervention. In the current literature, bulk modifications have not resolved the problem, and no study has yet demonstrated a reliable, protective surface barrier tailored specifically to deter molten-aluminum attack on boride-based systems.
decision.lever: apply a thin, dense diffusion‐barrier coating (e.g., a silicide or advanced ceramic layer) via a controlled deposition technique such as physical vapor deposition or pack cementation
decision.why: Recent trends indicate that shifting from bulk composition changes to targeted interface engineering—where a protective layer is applied to inhibit interdiffusion and chemical attack—offers a promising route to improve high‐temperature corrosion resistance. Supporting evidence from systems like refractory alloys coated with silicide layers demonstrates improved oxidation/corrosion behavior, making this intervention the most plausible next step to specifically address molten-aluminum corrosion on boride-based components.
